articles.title: Roadworks on Manchester Road Old Section to begin on 25 October 2026
articles.excerpt: Temporary closure of part of Manchester Road Old Section in Rochdale from 25 October 2026 due to roadworks.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has announced that roadworks will commence on the Old Section of Manchester Road from 25 October 2026. The work is expected to last until 30 October 2026, or until completion if sooner.

The affected area will see a temporary closure starting 1 metre north of the junction with Castle Avenue, extending 10 metres further north. This closure will impact traffic flow, particularly for those using this section of the road.

Motorists and local residents should plan their journeys accordingly, as diversions may be necessary during the roadworks. The council has provided a map of the roadworks and restrictions on their website for those seeking further details.

This development is significant for local commuters and residents, as it may affect access to nearby businesses and homes. For the latest updates and to view the roadworks map, visit the Rochdale Borough Council website.

articles.title: Rochdale Council awards contract for Queen's Park SEND improvement project
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract to enhance the play area at Queen's Park, Heywood, focusing on inclusivity for children with special educational needs.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract to MASSEY & HARRIS (ENGINEERING) LIMITED for the Queen's Park SEND and Improvement Project. This initiative aims to create a more inclusive play area at Queen's Park in Heywood, enhancing facilities for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND).

The project will involve several key improvements, including the extension of the existing play area, the installation of a dance arch, the creation of a sensory area surrounding the dance arch, and the addition of a wheelchair swing. These enhancements are designed to ensure that all children can enjoy the park's facilities, regardless of their physical abilities.

The decision to improve the play area reflects the council's commitment to inclusivity and accessibility in public spaces. By investing in these facilities, Rochdale Council aims to provide a safe and engaging environment for all children in the community, promoting social interaction and play.

The next steps will involve the commencement of construction works, with further updates expected as the project progresses. This development is significant for local families, particularly those with children who have SEND, as it will provide them with improved recreational opportunities in their community.

articles.title: Two Rochdale men among ten charged in drugs supply investigation
articles.excerpt: GMP says two Rochdale men are among ten people charged following a seven-month investigation. All ten have been remanded ahead of a Crown Court appearance.
articles.content_html:
Two Rochdale men are among ten people charged following a seven-month investigation into the suspected supply and distribution of drugs across Greater Manchester and the West Midlands.

Greater Manchester Police named the local defendants as Jailil Ahmed, 53, of Twinegate, Rochdale, and Shakil Ahmed, 51, of Whittaker Lane, Rochdale.

In a statement issued on 27 October, the force said eight men, a woman and a 16-year-old boy had been charged with conspiracy to supply controlled drugs in classes A, B and C, and conspiracy to supply an unauthorised medicinal product.

The boy cannot be named for legal reasons. The other adult defendants are from Burnage and Wolverhampton, or have no fixed abode, according to the police statement.

GMP said its Serious and Organised Crime Group carried out the investigation into suspected large-scale supply and distribution in the two regions.

All ten have been remanded in custody ahead of a scheduled appearance at Manchester Crown Court on Friday 13 November 2026, the force said.

The charges are allegations. No finding of guilt should be inferred, and all defendants are presumed innocent unless and until convicted.

Middleton is making final preparations for its Christmas lights switch-on event, scheduled for Saturday, November 14, in Middleton Gardens. The festive atmosphere is already taking shape with decorations appearing throughout the town, including a special red shoe outside Middleton Library in memory of Rochdale Council officer Lauren Mason, who passed away two years ago.

The switch-on event will begin at 12pm and will feature a variety of attractions designed to engage the community and spread festive cheer. Attendees can look forward to food and drink stalls, fairground rides, and market stalls, including the Teenage Market, which supports local young entrepreneurs. Additionally, The Art House will host personalised Christmas card-making sessions and face painting for children.

As the day progresses, visitors will enjoy performances from local community groups, culminating in a performance by Middleton Brass Band at 4.30pm, which will help set the festive mood ahead of the lights being switched on.

This event not only marks the start of the Christmas season in Middleton but also provides an opportunity for local businesses and young entrepreneurs to showcase their offerings. Residents and visitors alike are encouraged to attend and participate in the festivities, making it a significant occasion for the community.

articles.title: Heywood prepares for Remembrance Day services on 8 November 2026
articles.excerpt: The borough of Rochdale will hold Remembrance Day services across various townships, inviting public participation to honour servicemen and women.
articles.content_html:
The borough of Rochdale is set to hold Remembrance Day services on Sunday, 8 November 2026, across various townships, including Heywood. The council has extended an invitation to all members of the public to attend these commemorative events, which aim to honour the sacrifices made by servicemen and women, both past and present.

In a statement, the Mayor of Rochdale expressed the importance of community solidarity during this time of remembrance. The council is committed to supporting all members of the armed forces community, ensuring that their contributions are recognised and appreciated by the public.

Poppies, a symbol of remembrance, can be purchased at Number One Riverside in Rochdale and other designated locations. Additionally, they are available for purchase online through the Royal British Legion's website. The public is encouraged to wear poppies as a mark of respect and gratitude towards those who have served in the armed forces.

As the date approaches, residents are reminded of the significance of Remembrance Day and the opportunity it provides to reflect on the sacrifices made for peace and freedom. The council looks forward to seeing a strong turnout from the community to pay their respects.

articles.title: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing updates on Representative Body developments
articles.excerpt: Andrew Johnson has been re-appointed as Chair of the RBH Representative Body, with Rachael Ray as Deputy Chair, as they work to improve services for residents.
articles.content_html:
Andrew Johnson has been re-appointed as Chair of the Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) Representative Body during a meeting held last week. He welcomed Rachael Ray as the new Deputy Chair and acknowledged the contributions of outgoing Deputy Chair Rob Dyson. This update was shared on October 27, 2026, and highlights the ongoing commitment of the Representative Body to enhance services for residents.

During the meeting, the Representatives approved RBH's Annual Report to Customers, which is available on the RBH website. Johnson expressed satisfaction that the Representatives were able to provide additional oversight before the report's publication. The body also approved the findings of a recent scrutiny review aimed at improving customer feedback regarding the investment programme.

The scrutiny review resulted in six out of seven recommendations being accepted, including tailored approaches for gathering feedback from different customer groups. Johnson thanked the panel members and RBH staff for their efforts in this review, which aims to enhance how the organisation interacts with its customers and manages services.

Membership in RBH allows residents to have a voice in shaping the services that affect their homes and communities. Johnson encouraged those not yet members to sign up, emphasizing that their involvement strengthens the organisation and ensures it remains responsive to the needs of the community.

articles.title: Hopwood Hall College celebrates topping out of new Clegg Building
articles.excerpt: A topping out ceremony at Hopwood Hall College marks a significant step in the construction of the new Clegg Building, set to enhance educational facilities in Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
A topping out ceremony was held at Hopwood Hall College on October 26, 2026, marking a significant milestone in the construction of the new Clegg Building. This event celebrated the completion of the building's structure, which is being developed by Willmott Dixon and funded by the Department for Education, Rochdale Council, and the college itself.

The ceremony was attended by notable figures including Principal and CEO Julia Heap OBE, Rochdale MP Paul Waugh, and the Mayor and Mayoress of Rochdale, Faisal Rana and Iram Faisal. Family members of the late Robert Clegg OBE, after whom the building is named, were also present, highlighting the personal connection to the college. Robert Clegg served as Chair of the Corporation from 2007 to 2018 and made significant contributions during his tenure.

During the event, attendees were taken to the roof of the new building, which offers panoramic views of the borough, including landmarks such as Rochdale Town Hall and St Chad’s Parish Church. Guests were invited to leave messages on the roof parapet, creating a lasting record of the occasion.

The Clegg Building is expected to provide a modern and inspiring learning environment for students at Hopwood Hall College, enhancing educational opportunities in the area. As construction progresses, the college community looks forward to the completion of this landmark development, which aims to foster a better learning experience for current and future students.

articles.title: Does a boggart still haunt Clegg Hall?
articles.excerpt: The house on Clegg Hall Road is real and protected, the boggart story is old — but the medieval “tragedy” that feeds the legend is not supported by contemporary records.
articles.summary: The house on Clegg Hall Road is real and protected, the boggart story is old — but the medieval “tragedy” that feeds the legend is not supported by contemporary records.
articles.body:
Short answer: there is no documentary proof that Clegg Hall was the scene of a medieval massacre and therefore no factual basis to claim a still‑active, historically verified haunting. The house that people call Clegg Hall survives as a recognisable historic building and the boggart tale survives as folklore recorded by Victorian collectors; the two things sit side by side, not one inside the other. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1309615))

What we can say with confidence about place and period is plainly written in the records. The standing house on Clegg Hall Road is Grade II* on the National Heritage List for England and is described there as a house of about 1610, probably built for Theophilus Ashton; the list entry records its form, materials and a National Grid Reference (SD 92242 14490). The List entry is concerned with architecture and history, not ghost stories. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1309615))

The boggart story — the thing people mean when they talk about “Clegg Hall” in the way they might say “that place is haunted” — is a well‑attested piece of Lancashire folklore. It was written down and popularised in the nineteenth century by folklorists and local balladists. John Roby included an extended narrative about the “Clegg‑Hall Boggart” in his Traditions of Lancashire, and nineteenth‑century collectors and compilers (and later commentators) preserved variants that add striking motifs: murdered heirs, demons walking the house, an exorcist who bargains for “a body and a soul” and then produces “the body of a cock and the sole of a shoe” as a trick to lay the spirits. Those details recur across Roby, local ballads and later folklore anthologies. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/25256/25256-h/25256-h.htm))

That still leaves a gap between colourful tale and verifiable fact. County historians who examined surviving deeds, visitations and surveys note that the estate’s documentary trail is ordinary land‑transaction history: the Clegg estates passed through Belfield, Howorth and other families, and the present house is likely a seventeenth‑century rebuild rather than a thirteenth‑ or fourteenth‑century timber manor in which a serial murder took place. The 1889 History of the Parish of Rochdale specifically warns that Roby’s dramatic narrative is “pure imagination” while acknowledging a living tradition of a ghost and even a local proverb, “As ill as Clegg Hall boggart,” meaning hard to get rid of. In short, land deeds and the Manor Survey (1626) document ownership and a substantial house; they do not record the alleged atrocity that underpins the legend. ([your-content.s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com](https://your-content.s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/04145039/chapter-xvii-old-houses-and-old-families-butterworth-pages337-389.pdf))

How historians and folklorists read that difference matters. Folklore scholars treat the Clegg Hall boggart as a regional example of a wider boggart tradition in Lancashire — mischievous, sometimes malevolent household spirits attached to particular places — and they trace how oral tale, ballad and antiquarian retelling built up the colourful episodes now associated with the site. Local‑history sources, by contrast, look for contemporary legal or parish records to corroborate dramatic claims and find none that support a medieval massacre. Both approaches are valid but answer different questions: one asks how people told and remembered the place, the other asks what can be proved from surviving documents. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/25256/25256-h/25256-h.htm))

So does a boggart still haunt Clegg Hall? If you mean “is there corroborated historical evidence of a medieval tragedy that left a ghost,” the answer is no. If you mean “does the story still haunt local memory and appear in collections and ballads?” the answer is yes — the tale is part of Rochdale‑area folklore and was repeatedly collected and retold in the nineteenth century and later. The difference is between living local tradition and verifiable historical fact. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/25256/25256-h/25256-h.htm))

If you want to pursue the matter further: the National Heritage List entry is the authoritative source for the building’s architecture and dating; nineteenth‑century folkloric accounts (Roby and others) are the primary sources for the boggart narrative; and county histories and deed records (summarised in the parish history) are the place to check whether documentary evidence exists for any supposed crime. The List entry and county history are the best starting points for anyone who prefers deeds to apparitions. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1309615))

articles.title: Littleborough defeat Trafford MV in ADM Lancs/Cheshire 2 clash
articles.excerpt: Littleborough secured a victory against Trafford MV, maintaining their position at the top of ADM Lancs/Cheshire 2 despite challenging weather conditions.
articles.content_html:
Littleborough Rugby Club faced Trafford MV in a challenging match in the ADM Lancs/Cheshire 2 league on Saturday, October 26, 2026. The match took place at Littleborough's home ground, where the team managed to secure a win despite adverse weather conditions, including heavy rain and strong winds.

Trafford MV entered the game with a number of key players unavailable due to injuries, which affected their performance. They initially took the lead with a try from Mica Dyos, making the score 5-0. However, Littleborough responded quickly, scoring a try and converting it to lead 7-5 at half-time.

In the second half, Littleborough capitalised on the weather and the slope of the pitch, scoring another try and a penalty to extend their lead to 15-7. They added a further try, bringing the score to 22-7, before Trafford MV managed to score again through Aaron Booth, who converted his own try, reducing the deficit to 22-12.

This victory keeps Littleborough at the top of the league, while Trafford MV slips further down the standings. The match highlights the challenges teams face during adverse weather conditions and the impact of player availability on performance.

articles.title: Rochdale foster carers recognised for supporting over 1,000 children
articles.excerpt: At an awards ceremony in Rochdale Town Hall, 34 foster families were honoured for their commitment to caring for vulnerable children, collectively fostering for 465 years.
articles.content_html:
Thirty-four foster families were honoured at the annual Foster Carer Celebration Awards held at Rochdale Town Hall, recognising their dedication to providing safe and nurturing homes for vulnerable children. Collectively, these families have fostered for an impressive 465 years, supporting over 1,020 children and young people from newborns to 18 years old.

Among those celebrated were Michael and Marilyn, a couple from Milnrow, who have fostered for 50 years since 1976. They have cared for over 330 children, primarily focusing on newborns and siblings. Marilyn expressed her love for fostering, stating, "How long is a piece of string?" when asked how long they would continue. She reflected on the joy of seeing children grow up and receiving letters from adoptive parents thanking them for their influence.

The event highlighted the vital role foster families play in the community, providing stability and care to those in need. The awards serve not only to recognise the individual contributions of these families but also to raise awareness about the importance of fostering in Rochdale.

This recognition is significant as it underscores the ongoing need for foster carers in the area. With many children still in need of stable homes, the event aims to inspire others in the community to consider fostering. For those interested in becoming foster carers, further information can be obtained from the local authority's fostering service.

An eight-year-old school pupil has won a competition to name a road for a new £6.4 million First Choice Homes Development in Heywood. Ava McEvoy put forward the name Murphy Close for the housing association’s 27-home Bury Old Road project in honour of a local Catholic priest. A panel of judges decided the year 4 student’s suggestion will now take pride of place at the development's entrance. Father Morris Murphy founded a parish for the Darnhill Estate in the 1960s and was a respected community figure until his death in 2013. Ava, who goes to Our Lady and St Paul's RC Primary School, received a Samsung tablet for her winning name. "I'm really happy that my street name was chosen," she said. "I picked Murphy Close because Father Murphy did so much for the local community, and I wanted people to remember him." Headteacher of Ava’s school, Hollie Aspinall added: "We are incredibly proud of Ava and all the pupils who took part in the competition. “It has been a fantastic opportunity for our children to learn about local history and feel connected to a development that will become part of their community. Congratulations to Ava on her well-deserved win." FCHO project and partnerships officer Ghazalla Ibqal said: "This competition has given local children the opportunity to leave a lasting mark on the neighbourhood while learning about the people and stories that have helped shape Heywood. “We'd like to thank the school for working with us and congratulate Ava on her fantastic entry." The Bury Old Road project by Built Developments for FCHO comprises 12 two-bedroom and 15 three-bedroom properties. Nineteen are for social rent and eight rent-to-buy. Completion is scheduled for May next year. The judging panel was FCHO chief executive Mark Gifford, FCHO construction manager Jamie Smith, Ghazalla Iqbal, Hollie Aspinall and local councillors Stuart Crawford and Peter Joinson. articles.title: Heywood nursery loses planning bid to keep caravan as outbuilding
articles.excerpt: Little Oaks Nursery in Heywood has been denied permission to retain a caravan used as an outbuilding, following a planning decision by Rochdale Council.
articles.content_html:
Little Oaks Nursery, located on Bamford Road in Heywood, has lost its bid to keep a caravan that replaced a temporary Portakabin in its yard. The nursery applied for retrospective planning permission for the caravan, which has been used as an outbuilding since the Portakabin was removed in 2024 after being granted temporary permission in 2022.

A report from a planning officer indicated that pre-application advice had been sought regarding the placement of a static caravan on the site. The advice stated that such a structure would not be visually appropriate and would be highly visible from both directions along Bamford Road. Despite this, the caravan was placed on the site without the necessary planning permission, prompting the nursery's application to regulate its presence.

The planning officer's report further noted that the caravan does not meet the high-quality design standards required for a permanent structure. It was concluded that the caravan does not offer any visual improvement over the temporary Portakabin it replaced, which was only accepted for a limited time due to its unsuitability for permanent retention.

This decision by Rochdale Council highlights ongoing concerns regarding planning regulations and the visual impact of structures within the area. Local residents and businesses may be affected by the enforcement of these regulations, as they aim to maintain the aesthetic integrity of the neighbourhood.

Little Oaks Nursery applied to Rochdale Council for retrospective planning permission for the caravan which is being used as an outbuilding at its site in Bamford Road, Heywood. It follows planning permission granted in 2022 for a temporary Portakabin classroom which was removed in 2024. A planning officer’s report said: “Simultaneously, pre-application advice was requested and given for the siting of a static caravan on the site. “The advice given was that such a structure would not be visually appropriate for the site and would be highly visible from both directions along Bamford Road. “Notwithstanding, it appears that a static caravan was nonetheless placed at the site without the benefit of planning permission and this application therefore seeks regulation of such. “The caravan does not provide the high-quality design that officers had previously stated would be required for a permanent structure. “In design terms, the caravan is of no visual improvement over the temporary Portakabin it replaces, which was accepted only for a temporary period on the basis that it was unacceptable for permanent retention. READ MORE: Remembrance Sunday services across the borough “The domestic, leisure-caravan character makes the structure even less suitable for permanent retention on the application site than a modular classroom would be. “Officers therefore consider that the visual harm that had been tolerated previously due to the transient and temporary nature of the development (being the Portakabin) is not acceptable in this instance where the structure would be of permanent nature.” Officers said that while the caravan is currently screened from view by fencing and a trellis, the trellis is a temporary measure and would require separate planning permission. The report added: “The unauthorised screening is insufficient to mitigate this harm, and the development is therefore contrary to policy.” Refusing the application, the council said: “The proposed development, by reason of its siting, massing, design, and temporary utilitarian appearance, would appear as an incongruous, poorly designed feature which would be readily visible from the surrounding street scene by virtue of its prominent location along Bamford Road. “The proposed development would fail to achieve high-quality design and would therefore be harmful to the visual amenities of the area. “The limited public benefits are insufficient to outweigh the harm caused and the proposed development is therefore contrary to Policies DM1 and P3 of the adopted Rochdale Core Strategy, Policy JP-P1 of the Places for Everyone Joint Development Plan, and the National Planning Policy Framework.” The nursery must remove the caravan or appeal the decision. articles.title: GTAS weekly guide brings Halloween fun and a remembrance walk to Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Get Together After Serving has shared its programme for 26 October to 1 November, including afternoon tea, a remembrance walk, Halloween activities and football.
articles.content_html:
Get Together After Serving has shared its weekly programme for 26 October to 1 November 2026, with afternoon tea, a remembrance walk and Halloween activities at Denehurst Café, alongside football fixtures.

The community group is encouraging people to come along, get involved and support its activities. Here is the programme supplied by GTAS.

Monday 26 October: Afternoon tea at Denehurst Café runs from 12.30pm to 2.30pm. Booking is required, so contact GTAS to check availability before attending.

Wednesday 28 October: The Remembrance and Reflection Walk offers a gentle amble around the park, with time to chat and reflect. Meet at Denehurst Café at 12.15pm, ready for a 12.30pm start. GTAS men’s nine a side team is also in action; the supplied programme does not give a kick off time or venue.

Friday 30 October: Halloween activities at Denehurst Café include a movie night at 5pm and a spooky dog walk at 6pm.

Saturday 31 October: GTAS lists Port Vale v Rochdale with a 12.30pm kick off. Its programme also suggests parking up, meeting at Denehurst Café and walking to the ground. The fixture description and those walking arrangements need clarification, so confirm the match venue and meeting details with GTAS before travelling.

Sunday 1 November: GTAS Men’s Sunday League kicks off at 11am, with the venue still to be confirmed. GTAS Ladies are listed at Saddleworth 3Ds FC with a 3.30pm kick off.

The programme offers opportunities to spend time with others locally, whether over tea, on a walk or through sport. Check the GTAS page for updates, booking information and any changes before setting out. Prices, movie details and booking contact information were not included in the supplied guide.

Which activity would you like to join? Share your thoughts in the comments and pass the guide on to someone who might enjoy coming along.

articles.title: Heights Lane roadworks to begin on 26 October 2026
articles.excerpt: Roadworks on Heights Lane in Rochdale will result in temporary closures from 26 October to 1 November 2026, affecting local traffic.
articles.content_html:
Heights Lane in Rochdale will undergo roadworks starting from Monday, 26 October 2026, until Sunday, 1 November 2026. The road will be temporarily closed from its junction with Knowsley Street to its junction with Mizzy Road during this period.

The roadworks are expected to take place daily from 8 am to 5 pm, which may cause disruptions for local residents and commuters. An alternative route will be available via Howard Street, Whitehall Street, and Quarry Street.

This initiative is part of ongoing efforts by Rochdale Borough Council to improve local infrastructure and ensure safer travel for all road users. Residents are encouraged to plan their journeys accordingly during the closure period.

For more information, residents can view a map of the roadworks on the Rochdale Borough Council website or check Google Maps for directions.
